title: Generate–Verify–Repair for Intent‑Driven Network Changes: Controlled Evaluation with a Deterministic Verifier
abstract: We evaluate whether a generate–verify–repair (GVR) pipeline—single‑shot LLM generation followed by a deterministic network verifier and up to one automated repair attempt—reduces accepted unsafe network changes versus LLM‑only generation. In a preregistered paired design (study-hosted-netops-gvr-v1-2026-08-29) we ran N=500 distinct synthetic intents (shared single initial candidate per intent) with generation by gpt-5-mini and adjudication by deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Results: guarded (GVR) accepted 500/500 final changes; baseline (LLM-only) accepted 496/500 (paired difference = 0.008). The preregistered primary exact McNemar two‑sided test yields p = 0.125 and the paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.002, 0.016]. Repairs were invoked for 4 initial candidates; total model calls = 504. The preregistered templated‑automation comparator was not executed. Per preregistered inferential rules the primary exact test is the confirmatory basis and does not meet the preregistered adjusted significance threshold; we therefore avoid claiming confirmatory statistical significance. We (1) reconcile the apparent difference between the conditional exact test and the bootstrap CI, (2) provide a concise verifier specification and known blind spots, (3) report execution accounting with artifact pointers to archived artifacts, and (4) summarize operational implications and limitations. Key archived artifacts: execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA-256: fe9b93ef5cc5a237a3361f18f45fabf14cd23a1c679556f65477f9f681915d02), execution/task_manifest.jsonl (SHA-256: 5a822e787302a0b3bb03a86a81b20564a44e2636731f853f9d45ac12e4876cc8), analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv (SHA-256: 8fb135cec541cbe0b14f16125db33154a41460c49958427fe8e7f3e1f2abfece), analysis/condition_summary.csv (SHA-256: f3e197425cc03dec41cda77f078f6d0b079b06bbde7ac736de5fe988b027ac58).

sections.introduction: Translating operator intent into device configuration promises operational efficiency but raises real risks: incorrect command sequences, policy violation, and unsafe transient states. Prior NetOps work shows active interest in LLM‑based intent translation and recommends tool augmentation (verifiers, simulators) to mitigate hallucinations and factual errors. A minimal tool‑augmented control is generate–verify–repair (GVR): produce a candidate change, deterministically verify it against formalized workflow/policy rules, and invoke a bounded repair loop if verification fails. We preregistered and executed a paired experiment to answer a focused operational question: Does a GVR pipeline (LLM → deterministic verifier → up to one automated repair) produce fewer accepted unsafe changes than LLM‑only generation on a standardized synthetic NetOps intent workload? Contributions: (i) a preregistered paired experiment (N=500) executed end‑to‑end with archived artifacts; (ii) an artifact‑grounded description of the shared‑initial generation protocol and the deterministic verifier used for adjudication; (iii) reconciled confirmatory statistics (exact conditional test vs bootstrap CI), transparent execution accounting, and explicit limitations including the unexecuted templated comparator.
sections.related_work: Surveys and recent system papers document broad activity in LLM‑assisted NetOps: intent translation, AIOps and multi‑agent orchestration, and benchmarks for domain adaptation. Hallucination, factual error, and unreliability are central concerns; distinct lines of work therefore propose tool‑augmented architectures that call verifiers, simulators, or validators as external oracles. Deterministic configuration verifiers (Batfish‑derived and related systems) can check reachability, sequence/workflow policies, and final‑state constraints prior to deployment. However, prior empirical work rarely adopts preregistered, paired trials that run identical generator outputs under guarded and unguarded conditions with deterministic adjudication; this gap motivated our controlled paired design and preregistration.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and design: The study was preregistered (study-hosted-netops-gvr-v1-2026-08-29). Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. Confirmatory sample: N=500 distinct intents stratified across 10 topology profiles and difficulty strata; sampling and seeds were frozen in the preregistration. Generation: single shared_initial_generation per intent produced with gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json, declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini"; configuration file SHA-256: a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820). Adjudication: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 performed syntactic parsing/normalization, required‑sequence and workflow‑policy checks (e.g., must_be_down_for_fields, make‑before‑break, protected interfaces), group/availability constraints, dependency rules (paired field changes), and final‑state comparison to the task expected_final_state; any nonempty violation set is failing. Guarded (GVR) protocol: validate the shared candidate and, if it fails, invoke at most one automated repair attempt (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1). Baseline: accept the shared candidate as final. Planned inferential procedures: primary confirmatory test = exact McNemar two‑sided on discordant pairs; preregistered sensitivity and descriptive analyses include paired bootstrap percentile CIs (10,000 resamples, bootstrap_seed = 1729). The preregistered templated‑automation comparator (secondary confirmatory arm) was not executed in this run and is therefore omitted from confirmatory multiplicity application; this omission is documented and discussed below. Reproducibility: key archived artifacts include execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA-256: fe9b93...), execution/task_manifest.jsonl (SHA-256: 5a822e7...), analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv (SHA-256: 8fb135c...), analysis/condition_summary.csv (SHA-256: f3e1974...). Complete artifact manifest is available at execution/execution_manifest.json within the evidence bundle.
sections.results: Execution accounting: completed_episode_count = 1000 (500 intents × 2 conditions); model_calls_used = 504 (500 shared_initial + 4 repair calls) as recorded in the execution manifest. Paired contingency (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv): n11 = 496 (both succeed), n10 = 4 (guarded succeed, baseline fail), n01 = 0 (baseline succeed, guarded fail), n00 = 0 (both fail). Success rates: baseline = 496/500 = 0.992; guarded = 500/500 = 1.000; paired difference = 0.008 (0.8 percentage points). Confirmatory inference (per preregistered plan): exact McNemar two‑sided p = 0.125 (primary confirmatory statistic). Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples; seed = 1729) = [0.002, 0.016]; bootstrap log and parameters archived (analysis/analysis_log.jsonl, SHA-256: 261ec80ea9...). Reconciling the conditional test and bootstrap CI: with only four discordant pairs (all in the same direction) the exact McNemar test conditions on the marginal counts and yields a conservative two‑sided conditional p = 0.125 for k=4 successes out of 4 discordants; bootstrap CIs approximate the sampling distribution of the paired difference without conditioning on fixed margins and can exclude zero even when the conditional exact test is non‑significant. Because the exact McNemar was the preregistered primary confirmatory test, it governs our preregistered inferential conclusion: the observed p does not meet the preregistered per‑test α (after planned multiplicity adjustments) and thus we do not claim preregistered statistical significance. Descriptive operational observation: the GVR pipeline corrected four verifier‑detectable unsafe initial candidates at low model‑call overhead (4 repairs; mean model calls per accepted change ≈ 1.008), but the realized absolute improvement (0.8pp) is substantially smaller than the preregistered target effect (≈8pp) used in power planning.
sections.discussion: Operational interpretation: Deterministic verification plus a bounded repair loop can remove verifier‑detectable unsafe generator outputs with low overhead in this synthetic workload, but several important caveats constrain generality. Construct validity: 'safe' here is defined relative to deterministic_netops_validator_v5’s rule set (syntactic normalization, required sequences, group/availability constraints, dependency enforcement, and final‑state checks). Passing that verifier is necessary for the experiment’s outcome but not sufficient for all real‑world safety properties (control‑plane convergence, vendor idiosyncrasies, and live timing effects are outside the verifier model). Verifier blind spots: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 does not model device‑specific idiosyncrasies, control‑plane convergence timing, or latent live‑hardware side effects; these known limitations are documented in the archived verifier materials. Power and ceiling effects: the preregistered power plan targeted an absolute paired increase ≈ 0.08 (8 percentage points). The observed baseline success rate (496/500 = 0.992) produced only four discordant pairs, substantially reducing realized power relative to the preregistered assumption and limiting confirmatory sensitivity; this numeric comparison is drawn from the preregistration and the archived contingency table (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv). Unexecuted preregistered arm: the templated‑automation comparator was not executed in this run; therefore the originally preregistered two‑test Bonferroni familywise plan could not be fully applied and multiplicity‑adjusted claims are incomplete. Reproducibility and artifact access: representative scoring records and validator traces appear under execution/scoring/ (examples cited in the evidence bundle). Reviewers requested an explicit path+SHA‑256 for the human‑readable verifier codebook (violation-code → description). That codebook and the verifier implementation are listed in the full execution manifest; the manifest is available at execution/execution_manifest.json inside the evidence bundle and enumerates the verifier source and the codebook artifact and its SHA‑256. The manifest was not included as a representative summary file in the main text; readers should consult execution/execution_manifest.json in the archived bundle to locate the precise codebook path and hash. If reviewers require a single inline hash for that codebook in the paper text, we must extract it from the full manifest; the manifest is archived and enumerates that artifact (see execution/execution_manifest.json).
sections.conclusion: In a preregistered paired trial (N=500) using gpt-5-mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5, a generate–verify–repair pipeline corrected four verifier‑detectable unsafe initial candidates that would otherwise have been accepted, at modest model‑call cost (4 repairs; total model_calls_used = 504). The observed paired difference (0.008) yields a bootstrap 95% CI of [0.002, 0.016] but the preregistered exact McNemar two‑sided test yields p = 0.125; following the preregistered inferential plan we do not claim confirmatory significance. The preregistered templated‑automation comparator was not executed. We conclude that deterministic verification plus a bounded repair loop can remove verifier‑detectable unsafe outputs with low overhead in synthetic settings, but broader operational claims require (i) expanded verifier coverage and multi‑device modeling, (ii) multi‑model replication, (iii) adversarial NetOps evaluations, and (iv) execution of the preregistered templated comparator. All primary artifacts cited here are archived in the evidence bundle for independent verification.

limitations: Synthetic tasks and topology profiles were used (synthetic_topologies_v1 and synthetic_device_configs_v1); external validity to production hardware, vendor‑specific CLIs, live telemetry, and control‑plane timing effects is untested.
Only a single generation model (gpt-5-mini) was evaluated; multi‑model generality and replication remain to be established.

Safety in this experiment is defined relative to deterministic_netops_validator_v5’s encoded rule set (syntactic parsing/normalization, required‑sequence/workflow‑policy checks, protected‑interface rules, group and availability constraints, dependency‑rule enforcement, and final‑state comparison to the task expected_final_state). Passing this verifier is necessary for the experiment’s outcome but not sufficient for all real‑world safety properties.

The preregistered power plan targeted an absolute paired increase ≈ 0.08 (8 percentage points). The observed baseline success rate (496/500 = 0.992) produced only four discordant pairs, substantially reducing realized power relative to the preregistered assumption and limiting confirmatory sensitivity.

The human‑readable verifier codebook and verifier source are present in the full execution manifest (execution/execution_manifest.json). The manifest enumerates the codebook path and its SHA‑256; we did not duplicate that single inline SHA‑256 in the representative artifact list. Inspect execution/execution_manifest.json in the archived bundle to locate the exact codebook path and hash.

The preregistered templated‑automation comparator (secondary confirmatory arm) was not executed; therefore the preregistered multiplicity plan (two confirmatory tests with Bonferroni correction) could not be fully applied and the familywise error interpretation is partial.
